title: Quality planning
blurb: Explain what quality planning produces: acceptance criteria, standards, methods and responsibilities, captured in a quality management plan.
question: A council is replacing its housing-repairs booking system. Tenants say it must be 'easy to use' and the IT team says it must be 'robust'. Before the build starts, what should the project manager do so the finished system can be objectively accepted, and where should this be recorded?

teach.body: APM describes quality as the fitness for purpose, or the degree of conformance, of the outputs of a process or of the process itself. In plain English: an output is 'quality' when it does the job it was meant to do and meets the requirements that were agreed. It does not mean luxury or the best money can buy. Quality management has four parts: quality planning, quality assurance, quality control and continuous improvement. Planning comes first, because you can't check quality until you've agreed what it is.

teach.h: The four parts of quality management
teach.caption: Planning defines 'good'. Assurance gives confidence in the process, control checks the outputs, and improvement feeds the lessons back in.

teach.body: Quality planning takes the defined scope and specifies the ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA that will show each output is fit for purpose, plus the STANDARDS to apply, the METHODS of checking, the RESPONSIBILITIES (who checks, who accepts) and the quality ACTIVITIES (reviews, tests, audits) and when they happen. All of this is recorded in a quality management plan. Why bother? Everyone agrees what 'good' looks like before work starts, so there are fewer disputes at handover, less rework and no gold plating.

teach.h: From a vague wish to a testable criterion

steps.label: Requirement
steps.sub: Tenants can book a repair online without help

steps.label:
Acceptance
criterion
steps.sub: 9 of 10 test tenants book a repair unaided in under 3 minutes

steps.label: Responsibility
steps.sub: Test lead runs it; the housing manager signs off

teach.caption: A criterion must be measurable and agreed in advance, or nobody can say objectively whether it has been met.

teach.h: Typical contents of a quality management plan
head: Section
What it covers
Repairs system example
rows: End of each stage; before go-live
teach.caption: A typical list, not a mandated APM template. The plan is part of the wider project management plan.

teach.body: Tenants want 'easy', the IT team wants 'robust' and the repairs manager wants it live before winter. The project manager runs a workshop with all three groups and turns each wish into a measurable criterion: booking unaided in under 3 minutes, 500 users at once with no errors, and the council's accessibility standard met. Where regulation sets a minimum and stakeholders want more, the plan records one combined baseline. Conflicts are resolved now, in planning, not argued over at handover.

teach.h: Quality planning in linear and iterative life cycles

rows.label: When planned
values: High level first, detail per time box

teach.caption: In an iterative life cycle time and cost are fixed and scope flexes. Agreed quality standards are not traded away to hit a date.

teach.text: Three classic traps. (1) Quality is NOT 'the highest standard possible': exceeding the requirements is gold plating, which adds cost without needed benefit. (2) In iterative projects quality does NOT flex: scope does. (3) Quality planning is not testing: planning DEFINES the criteria, quality control later CHECKS outputs against them.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Define it: quality planning takes the scope and specifies how fitness for purpose will be shown.
Name the contents: acceptance criteria, standards, methods, responsibilities and quality activities, in a quality management plan.
Show how: engage stakeholders to turn vague expectations into measurable, testable criteria and resolve conflicts early.
Give the why: shared view of 'good', objective acceptance, less rework and fewer disputes, no gold plating.
Apply it to the scenario and, if asked, contrast linear (up front) with iterative (per feature, per time box).
Quality = fitness for purpose: meeting agreed requirements, not luxury.
Quality planning turns scope into acceptance criteria, standards, methods, responsibilities and activities.
It is recorded in the quality management plan, part of the project management plan.
Good acceptance criteria are measurable, agreed with stakeholders and set before work starts.
Linear: planned up front. Iterative: criteria per feature each time box, and quality never flexes.

summary: You can now explain what quality planning is and what a quality management plan contains. You can also turn a vague expectation into a measurable acceptance criterion and explain how quality planning differs between linear and iterative life cycles.

A.q: Which of the following BEST describes what quality planning produces?
options: Acceptance criteria, standards, methods and responsibilities
Inspection results showing which outputs passed or failed
An independent audit of whether processes are being followed
A record of defects found and the rework needed to fix them
A.why: Quality planning takes the scope and specifies the acceptance criteria, standards, methods and responsibilities (plus quality activities), recorded in the quality management plan.

whyNot.1: Inspection results come from quality control, which happens after planning.
whyNot.2: An independent process audit is quality assurance, not planning.
whyNot.3: Defect and rework records are produced by quality control as outputs are checked.

A.q: A stakeholder says a new staff intranet must simply be 'fast'. What should the project manager do during quality planning?
options: Accept the term and let the testers judge speed later
Reject it, because speed is subjective and cannot be measured
Agree a measurable target, such as pages loading in 2 seconds
Ask the supplier to apply its own definition of 'fast'
A.why: Quality planning converts vague expectations into measurable acceptance criteria agreed with stakeholders, so the output can be objectively checked.

whyNot.0: Leaving it vague means testers and users will disagree at acceptance, causing disputes and rework.
whyNot.1: Speed can be measured; the expectation is valid and just needs translating into a criterion.
whyNot.3: The supplier's definition may not match the users' need; criteria should be agreed with stakeholders.

A.q: Which document normally records the standards, acceptance criteria and quality responsibilities for a project?
options: The benefits management plan
The procurement strategy
The communication plan
The quality management plan
A.why: The quality management plan sets out how quality will be achieved and checked: standards, acceptance criteria, methods, responsibilities and activities.

whyNot.0: The benefits management plan covers how benefits will be defined, tracked and realised.
whyNot.1: The procurement strategy sets out how goods and services will be bought from suppliers.
whyNot.2: The communication plan covers who receives what information, when and how.

B.q: Why should acceptance criteria be agreed BEFORE work on a deliverable starts?
options: So the testing team can decide later how strict to be
So everyone knows in advance what 'acceptable' looks like
So the supplier can lower the standard if costs rise
So the sponsor no longer needs to approve the final outputs
B.why: Agreeing criteria up front gives everyone a shared, objective view of 'acceptable', so the work is built to it and acceptance is clear.

whyNot.0: Criteria are set in planning; leaving strictness to testers later creates ambiguity.
whyNot.2: Agreed criteria protect the standard; lowering it would need formal change control.
whyNot.3: Criteria make approval objective; they don't remove the need for it.

B.q: A care home extension must meet fire-safety regulations, and the client also wants sound insulation well above the legal minimum. What should the quality plan set out?
options: One baseline meeting the regulations plus the client's extras
The regulations only, as legal duties always override clients
The client's wishes only, because the client funds the work
Whichever of the two standards is cheaper to deliver
B.why: The plan should combine both: regulatory standards as the compulsory minimum, plus the client's agreed requirements, in one baseline.

whyNot.1: Legal duties must be met, but the client's agreed extra requirements are part of fitness for purpose too.
whyNot.2: Regulations cannot be ignored just because the client is paying.
whyNot.3: Cost alone doesn't decide quality: both the legal minimum and agreed requirements must be met.

B.q: On an iterative app project the time box is running short. Which statement about quality is correct?
options: Quality criteria can be relaxed so the deadline is met
The time box end date is extended until every feature is done
Testing is postponed to a later time box to save time
Lower-priority features are dropped; quality is protected
B.why: In an iterative life cycle time and cost are fixed and scope flexes (by priority). Agreed quality standards are protected.

whyNot.0: Quality is not what flexes: relaxing criteria would deliver features that are not fit for purpose.
whyNot.1: Time boxes have fixed end dates; scope flexes instead.
whyNot.2: Features are tested within the time box; postponing testing builds up hidden defects.

C.q: Which of the following is the MAIN benefit of involving users when acceptance criteria are set?
options: Criteria reflect what users actually need from the outputs
Users can take over the project manager's quality duties
The project no longer needs any formal testing before handover
Users accept responsibility for funding any later rework
C.why: Users know what 'fit for purpose' means in practice. Without them, outputs can meet the specification yet fail their needs.

whyNot.1: The project manager remains responsible for managing quality; users contribute requirements and acceptance.
whyNot.2: Criteria define what testing must prove; they don't remove the need to test.
whyNot.3: Users don't fund rework; involving them is about getting the criteria right.

C.q:
Which TWO of the following are typical contents of a quality management plan?
1. Acceptance criteria for key deliverables
2. The investment appraisal for the project
3. Responsibilities for quality checks and sign-off
4. The stakeholder power/interest grid
options: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
C.why: A quality management plan sets out acceptance criteria, standards, methods, responsibilities and the schedule of quality activities.

whyNot.0: The investment appraisal (2) belongs in the business case, not the quality plan.
whyNot.2: Neither the investment appraisal (2) nor the power/interest grid (4) belongs in the quality plan.
whyNot.3: The power/interest grid (4) is a stakeholder analysis tool, not quality plan content.

C.q: A sponsor asks for a new website to be 'the best on the market', well beyond the agreed requirements, with no extra budget. In quality terms, what is the main risk?
options: Quality assurance will become weaker
Acceptance criteria can't be written
Gold plating that adds unneeded cost
Users will reject outputs that work
C.why: Quality means fitness for purpose. Going beyond the agreed requirements is gold plating: extra cost and time for no needed benefit.

whyNot.0: The process assurance arrangements are not what this request threatens.
whyNot.1: Criteria can still be written; the problem is that the target exceeds the need.
whyNot.3: Users accept outputs that meet the agreed criteria; the risk is over-delivery, not rejection.

reteach.title: Ordering a wedding cake
reteach.question: You're ordering a wedding cake. How do you make sure the cake that arrives on the day is the one you wanted, with no arguments with the baker?

blocks.body: 'Something lovely' is a wish, not a criterion. A sensible couple agrees the details up front: three tiers, serves 120, lemon sponge, nut-free, matches the photo, delivered by 2pm. They agree a tasting session (the method of checking), who decides at the tasting (responsibility), and the baker's food hygiene rating (a standard). That agreement is their quality plan. If it's written down before baking, the cake on the day can be checked against it, not argued about.

blocks.text: A gold-leaf, seven-tier cake for 120 guests isn't 'higher quality' if three tiers were agreed: it's gold plating. Quality is meeting the agreed criteria.

explain.body: Quality is the fitness for purpose, or degree of conformance, of outputs (or of a process). A basic but reliable system that meets every agreed requirement is high quality. A luxurious one that misses a requirement is not.

test.q: In project management, quality is BEST described as:
options: Using the highest-grade materials and methods available
Delivering outputs with zero defects of any kind
Outputs that are fit for purpose and meet requirements
Whatever the most senior stakeholder considers best
test.why: Quality is fitness for purpose: outputs that conform to the agreed requirements.

whyNot.0: Highest grade isn't the aim; exceeding requirements is gold plating.
whyNot.1: Zero defects is rarely realistic; minor defects may be within agreed acceptance criteria.
whyNot.3: Quality is defined by agreed requirements, not one person's preference.

explain.body: Acceptance criteria are the measurable conditions an output must meet before it is accepted. They are agreed with stakeholders in quality planning, before the work starts, so acceptance is objective. Test each one: could two people measure it and agree on the result?

test.q: Which is the BEST example of an acceptance criterion for a new staff training course?
options: The course should be engaging and modern
85% of trainees pass the end-of-course test
The trainer should be experienced and friendly
The materials should look professional
test.why: It is specific and measurable, so anyone can check objectively whether it has been met.

whyNot.0: 'Engaging and modern' is subjective: people would disagree on whether it was met.
whyNot.2: 'Experienced and friendly' describes the trainer, and is not measurable as written.
whyNot.3: 'Professional' is a matter of opinion unless it is defined against a standard.

explain.body: The quality management plan records how quality will be achieved and checked: objectives, standards, acceptance criteria, methods, responsibilities, the schedule of reviews, tests and audits, and how records and failures are handled. It sits within the project management plan.

test.q: What is the main purpose of the quality management plan?
options: To prove to auditors that no defects were found
To list every defect fixed during the project
To replace the need for a separate project management plan
To set out how quality will be achieved and checked
test.why: The quality management plan sets out how quality will be achieved and checked: criteria, standards, methods, responsibilities and activities.

whyNot.0: It is written before the work, to plan quality; it doesn't prove results.
whyNot.1: Defects are recorded in quality control records, such as a defect log.
whyNot.2: It is part of the project management plan, not a replacement for it.

explain.body: Linear: quality is planned up front in definition, criteria are set per deliverable and acceptance happens at gates and handover. Iterative: high-level standards first, then criteria for each feature before it is built, with the product owner accepting or rejecting work each time box. Scope flexes; quality does not.

test.q: In an iterative project, who typically accepts or rejects completed features at the end of each time box?
options: The product owner
The external auditor
The PMO quality lead
The finance manager
test.why: The product owner represents the business and users, and accepts or rejects completed work each iteration against the agreed criteria.

whyNot.1: An external auditor gives independent assurance on processes; they don't accept features.
whyNot.2: A PMO quality lead may support assurance, but acceptance sits with the product owner.
whyNot.3: The finance manager has no role in accepting product features.
